about: "Make it specific" prompts for unit-6 (docs/aphug-architecture.md, "Make it specific"); checked by checkJustify in scripts/lib/aphug-exams.mjs.

prompts.title: Describing squatter settlements
prompts.prompt: Describe the favelas on the hillsides of Rio de Janeiro.
checklist: Names where they are, with a named favela
Says how homes were built and what services are like
Goes beyond the word "poor"

earns.answer: In Rio de Janeiro, favelas such as Rocinha climb the steep hillsides near wealthy beach neighborhoods; residents built the homes themselves without legal title, packed close together, often with weak access to sewers and roads.
earns.why: It names a place and describes where, how and with what services.

misses.answer: Favelas are poor neighborhoods in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.
misses.why: "Poor" alone is a label: describe where they are and what they are like.

why.1: The CBD holds offices and shops.
why.2: Favelas are inside the city.

why.1: Residents built them without legal title.
why.2: Developers build formal housing.

prompts.title: How situation helped Istanbul grow
prompts.prompt: Explain how its situation helped Istanbul grow into a great city.
checklist: Names Istanbul's situation: on the Bosporus
Says what that position links
Links it to trade and growth

earns.answer: Istanbul sits on the Bosporus, between Europe and Asia and between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, so for centuries ships and traders passed through it, which brought wealth, people and power to the city.
earns.why: It names the situation and links it, step by step, to growth.

misses.answer: Istanbul is on the Bosporus between Europe and Asia.
misses.why: That locates it but never says how the location helped it grow.

concept.label: Situation
options: on the Bosporus between two seas

why.1: Flat land is part of a site, not a situation.
why.2: Climate is part of the site.

why.1: Istanbul grew into a great city.
why.2: It was on the route, so ships came through.

prompts.title: Burgess and Hoyt
prompts.prompt: Compare the concentric zone model and the sector model, using Chicago.
checklist: Gives one similarity between the two models
Says how each arranges land use
Uses Chicago for at least one side

earns.answer: Both models start from a CBD, but the concentric zone model draws rings of land use around it, whereas the sector model draws wedges along transport lines, as in Chicago, where high-rent housing ran north along the lakeshore.
earns.why: It gives a similarity and a difference, with Chicago as evidence.

misses.answer: The concentric zone model has rings around the CBD.
misses.why: One side only: say how the sector model differs.

why.1: Wedges are the sector model.
why.2: Several centers is multiple nuclei.

why.1: Rings are the concentric zone model.
why.2: That is the galactic city.

prompts.title: How well Burgess fits Atlanta
prompts.prompt: Explain the degree to which the concentric zone model fits metro Atlanta.
checklist: States the degree first: to a low degree, for example
Gives evidence from Atlanta: growth along highways and edge cities
Names the model that fits better

earns.answer: To a low degree: metro Atlanta grew along highways in the car era, with offices and malls in edge cities such as Perimeter Center rather than in even rings around downtown, so the galactic city model fits it better.
earns.why: It states the degree, gives evidence and names a better fit.

misses.answer: Atlanta does not have perfect rings around its downtown.
misses.why: No degree stated, and no evidence of what Atlanta has instead.

why.1: Atlanta grew along highways, not in rings.
why.2: No real city fits a model exactly.

why.1: That model is for Latin American cities.
why.2: Von Thünen is about farm rings.

prompts.title: Naming a place: smart growth
prompts.context: A student writes: "Some cities use transit to cut car use."
prompts.prompt: Rewrite the claim with a real city, what it built and when.
checklist: Names a real city and what it built
Gives the year the project opened
Says the result for how people travel

earns.answer: Curitiba, Brazil, opened bus rapid transit lanes in 1974 and zoned dense housing along them, so many residents ride the bus instead of driving.
earns.why: It names the city, the project, the year and the result.

misses.answer: Some cities in South America built buses to reduce traffic.
misses.why: No city, no year and no specific project.

why.1: A continent, not a city.
why.2: That names no city.

kind.label: What it built
options: bus rapid transit lanes with dense housing

why.1: Highways invite more car use.
why.2: An airport does not cut city car trips.

prompts.title: Income at two scales in one city
prompts.prompt: Explain how income data for Washington, D.C., change from the scale of the whole city to the local scale of census tracts.
checklist: Says what the citywide figure shows
Names where tract data show lower incomes
Explains what the citywide figure hides

earns.answer: For the city as a whole, Washington, D.C., has a high median household income, but at the local scale, census tracts east of the Anacostia River, in Wards 7 and 8, have much lower incomes, so the citywide figure hides deep differences between neighborhoods.
earns.why: It names both scales, a place and what the larger figure hides.

misses.answer: Washington, D.C., has rich and poor neighborhoods.
misses.why: True, but no scale is named and no place is given.

why.1: Global data compare countries.
why.2: National data are coarser than the city.

why.1: The Mall is parkland and museums.
why.2: Tracts differ a great deal.

prompts.title: The limit of a one-night count
prompts.context: US cities count the people experiencing homelessness on one night in January each year (a point-in-time count).
checklist: Names who the count misses
Says why one night misses them
Says which way the count is off

earns.answer: A count on one night misses people staying with friends, in cars or in places counters do not reach, and people who are homeless at other times of year, so it likely understates how many people are homeless over a year.
earns.why: It names who is missed, why and which way the count errs.

misses.answer: Counting people is hard, so the numbers in the count might be wrong.
misses.why: Too vague: it names no group the count misses and no reason why.

limit.label: Who is missed
options: people staying with friends or in cars

why.1: Shelters are where the count is easiest.
why.2: Double counts make totals too high, the opposite problem.

why.1: Missing people makes the count too low.
why.2: One night cannot be exact for a year.

prompts.title: Rank-size and Lima
prompts.context: In Peru's 2017 census, Lima had about 9.5 million people and Arequipa, the second city, about 1 million (INEI).
prompts.prompt: Explain how well the rank-size rule fits Peru, and give one limit of the rule.
checklist: Says what the rule predicts for the second city
Compares it with Arequipa's real size
Names Lima's pattern and a limit of the rule

earns.answer: The rule fits Peru poorly: it predicts a second city half Lima's size, about 4.75 million, but Arequipa had about 1 million in 2017 (INEI), so Lima is a primate city, far more than twice the second; the rule cannot explain why power and jobs concentrate in one city.
earns.why: It computes the prediction, compares it with the data and gives a limit.

misses.answer: Lima is a primate city because it is the capital.
misses.why: It names the pattern but never tests the rule against the numbers.

why.1: Rank 2 is half of rank 1.
why.2: That is Arequipa's real size, not the rule's prediction.

why.1: Arequipa is far below the rule's prediction.
why.2: Central place theory is about spacing, not this size gap.

prompts.title: Reading a rent-burden legend
prompts.context: A map of census tracts in invented Capital City shades each tract by the share of renter households that pay more than 30% of their income on rent: under 20%, 20% to 34%, 35% to 49%, and 50% or more (invented data for practice).
prompts.prompt: Explain what a tract in the darkest class tells you, and what it does not.
checklist: Reads the class: half or more of renters pay over 30%
Says what that means for families there
Says the legend shows a share, not a count of people

earns.answer: In a tract in the darkest class, half or more of renter households pay more than 30% of their income on rent, so housing costs press hard on many families there; the legend shows a share of renters, not how many people live in the tract.
earns.why: It reads the class, interprets it and says what it does not show.

misses.answer: Rent is high in the darkest tracts on the map.
misses.why: The map is about the share of income spent on rent, not the rent itself, and no number is read.

data.label: Darkest class
options: half or more of renters pay over 30%

why.1: The legend is a share of income, not a price.
why.2: The legend is about rent burden, not renting.

limit.label: What it does not show
options: how many people live in the tract

why.1: Every tract is shaded, so all have data.
why.2: That is what it shows.

prompts.title: How redlining shaped neighborhoods
prompts.prompt: Explain how redlining in US cities from the 1930s shaped neighborhoods.
checklist: Says what redlining was: refusing or worsening loans by location
Names whom it fell on, historically
Links it to the effect on homes and values

earns.answer: From the 1930s, maps graded neighborhoods for lending risk, and lenders refused loans or offered worse terms in areas marked red, which were often Black and immigrant neighborhoods, so owners there could not borrow to buy or repair homes, which held down home values for decades.
earns.why: It defines the mechanism, names the history and links it to the effect.

misses.answer: Redlining was unfair to some neighborhoods.
misses.why: A judgment, not an explanation: no mechanism and no effect.

cause.label: What it was
options: refusing loans or worse terms by location

why.1: Highways are a different process.
why.2: That is redistricting.

effect.label: Effect
options: owners could not borrow, so values stayed low

why.1: Without loans, values were held down.
why.2: Lenders avoided those areas.
